title: Sunny Deol and Rajkumar Santoshi Reunite After Three Decades. Batwara 1947 Is the Partition Epic the Diaspora Has Been Bracing For.
excerpt: Aamir Khan narrates, A.R. Rahman scores, Shabana Azmi and Preity Zinta star — and in the teaser's most-shared line, Sunny growls: 'Iraada toh nahi, par aitraaz bhi nahi hai.'
body:
It opens, as the best Partition stories do, with a voice rather than a face. **Aamir Khan** — unseen, grave, almost mournful — talks us through the British Raj and the line that was about to be drawn across a subcontinent. Then the screen catches fire. Riots in the streets of a Pakistan that no longer knows what to do with its Hindus. An old woman, played by **Shabana Azmi**, stranded in the middle of it. And a family, fleeing the wrong way down history, walking straight into the inferno.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=DstkbSnWFf4</youtube>

That family is led by **Sunny Deol** — and if you grew up on **Ghayal**, **Damini** and **Ghatak**, the back of your neck just prickled. Because the man holding the camera is **Rajkumar Santoshi**, and the last time these two stood on a set together, the internet didn't exist. Thirty years. That's how long the diaspora's favourite righteous-rage pairing has been apart. The teaser for **Batwara 1947**, dropped on June 18 ahead of an Independence-Day-weekend release, exists mostly to remind you of that fact, and it lands like a fist.

The one-minute-five-second cut is not interested in plot. It's interested in feeling — fear, displacement, the specific terror of belonging nowhere. Santosh Sivan's camera moves through mass migration and shattered homes with the unhurried confidence of a man who knows exactly how good his frames are. **A.R. Rahman**'s background score does what Rahman does, swelling underneath the violence until the grief feels almost unbearable. And then Sunny Deol arrives, is asked the eternal Sunny Deol question — *"Panga lena hai?"* (You want a fight?) — and answers with the line that has already been screenshotted into oblivion:

> "Iraada toh nahi, par aitraaz bhi nahi hai." — Sunny Deol's character, Batwara 1947

I don't want trouble, but I won't object to it either. It is the most Sunny Deol sentence ever written, and X lost its mind. *"1000 cr is done and dusted,"* one user declared within hours. He may not be wrong.


Here's why this one matters more than the average teaser. **Batwara 1947** — which began life under the title **Lahore 1947** before the rename in early June — is adapted from Asghar Wajahat's celebrated play *Jis Lahore Nai Vekhya, O Jamya E Nai*, a text that has haunted Indian theatre for years precisely because it refuses the easy villain. It's the story of a Hindu woman who won't leave Lahore and the Muslim family that ends up protecting her. Santoshi, a National Award winner, is reaching past the action-hero register that made him and Deol famous and toward something closer to elegy. The supporting bench is stacked: **Preity Zinta**, returning to the screen and calling this the hardest film of her career; **Karan Deol**; **Ali Fazal**; and **Abhimanyu Singh** as the face of the mob. Javed Akhtar writes the lyrics. Aamir Khan produces alongside Aparna Purohit, and lends only his voice — a restraint that, for the industry's most famous perfectionist, counts as its own kind of statement.

The casting alone makes this a must-watch, but the timing is the masterstroke. **Batwara 1947** opens worldwide on **August 14, 2026** — the eve of Independence Day, the literal anniversary of the wound the film is about. For Sunny Deol, riding the **Gadar 2** and **Border 2** wave, it cements an extraordinary late-career run as the diaspora's patriot-in-chief. For a generation of NRIs whose grandparents crossed that border with nothing, it is something heavier than a movie.

**Where to watch, diaspora edition:** Batwara 1947 gets a worldwide theatrical release on August 14, 2026, distributed by PVR Inox. Expect wide bookings in the US, UK, Canada and Australia through the usual desi-cinema chains — partition dramas with this pedigree travel, and a long-weekend Independence Day window is built for exactly the Friday-night-with-the-whole-family outing that Sunny Deol films were made for. A streaming home hasn't been announced; given the theatrical scale and Aamir Khan Productions' patience with its catalogue, don't expect an OTT drop before late 2026 at the earliest.

Three decades is a long time to wait for two men to stand on a set again. The teaser suggests it was worth it.
